headline: TO-DAY'S WEDDING.
text:
PRETTY KOWLOON CEREMONY

Union Church, Kowloon, was the scene of a pretty wedding this afternoon, the parties being Miss Ida Mary Webb, daughter of Capt. and Mrs. C. E. Webb, and Mr. Austen Spary, of the Electrical department, P.W.D., son of Mrs. Spary and the late Lieut. Spary, R.E.

The bride, who was given away by her uncle, Mr. H. Stainfield, was prettily attired in a dress of white satin and georgetta trimmed with beads and orange blossom. Her bouquet was of white chrysanthemums and roses.

Miss Nancy McEwen, the brides-maid, wore a charming dress of blue crepe de chine and georgette with hat to match and her bouquet was also of white chrysanthemums and roses.

Mrs. C. E. Webb, mother of the bride, was matron of honour and her dress was of champagne crepe de chine trimmed with beads.

The Rev. J. Horace. Johnston officiated, Mr. D. W. Waterton was best man and Mr. Charles E. Terry was groomsman.

After the ceremony a reception was held at the home of the bride's parents at 3 Ley's Buildings and the bride and bridegroom are to leave for their honeymoon at Macao, the bride's travelling dress being a grey costume with hat and wrap coat to match.

The bride's gift to the bride-groom was a silver cigarette case and that of the bridegroom to the bride a slave bangle. Numerous costly presents were received by the young couple.

headline: BOYCOTT MODIFIED. / CANTON'S NEW IMPORT SYSTEM.
text:
FOREIGN TRADE RULES

As quoted by the “Canton Gazette,” the Strike Executive has agreed that “the regulations restricting the importation of foreign goods formerly, were too strict for the merchants.”

The Executive says: "So as to express our friendly feelings between the labourers and merchants, we draw up a modified system of imports." The modifications published are:—

(1) Cargo of non-British manufacture that come directly from Shanghai, although they are marked with the word "Hongkong," are allowed to be imported.

(2) Goods of non-British manufacture which have been stored in Hongkong and transhipped to Shanghai for shipment to Canton by another steamer, are allowed to be imported, if they are proved to be in accordance with our regulations, by any bill of lading and customs permit.

(3) Goods of all countries, even of non-British manufacture, if inscribed with the word “Hongkong,” when transhipped to Canton from the coastal ports of Kwangtung, namely, Swatow, Hainan, Kwang Chow Wan, etc., are considered infringements of our rules.

headline: SNATCHER CAUGHT.
text:
PORTUGUESE LADY ROBBED

ACCUSED SHIVERS IN COURT.

An elderly Chinese, describing himself as a shop employee, was smartly caught by European Sergeant Pointz just as the man was disappearing down a side street after a chase of 40 yards along Queen's Road Central. The reason for the hurried flight was that the man had purloined a Portuguese lady's handbag.

While out shopping in Queen's Road, Miss Amelia Maria Remedios, of No. 18, Jordan Road, Kowloon, noticed the man walking behind her and eyeing her handbag suspiciously. With his limping gait he was thought to be a beggar and no notice was taken of him. Seizing his opportunity the man snatched the handbag and ran away with it, but simultaneously with the alarm being raised the Sergeant was behind him.

Charged at the Central Magistracy this morning before Mr. R. E. Lindsell with committing a felony, the evidence was all against the defendant. He attempted to enlist the Magistrate's sympathy and evade punishment by shivering in Court and showing symptoms of apoplexy. His Worship deferred sentence to enable defendant's physical condition to be ascertained.

headline: NOTABLE ADVANCES.
text:
AMERICA ELIMINATES WASTE.

PROSPERITY OF INDUSTRY.

The annual report issued by Mr. Hoover, emphasises the progress of American industries in eliminating waste.

The country has also benefited by notable advances in science and the improvement in methods of management and prohibition. Thus it has the highest real wage in its history and has had a three years remarkable price stability. Mr. Hoover recommends a radical reduction in fees for passport and visas, the simplification of formalities in the appointment of competent officers to measure tonnage of vessels; and the uniform application of American measurement and regulations so as to prevent discrimination against American vessels, and the enactment of load-line legislation similar to that of European maritime powers.

headline: COTTON GAMBLING.
text:
BANKRUPTCY. FOR OLDHAM FIRM

The Lancashire cotton trade has been startled by the announcement of a liquidator for the cotton mills company at Oldham. That company has lost at least £3,500,000, largely by gambling in cotton figures and actual cotton. It is proposed to form a new company to take over the present company's mills at a price of £600,000.

headline: FROM FAR EAST
text:
THROUGH ROUTE ACROSS SIBERIA.

The international railway conference has opened to discuss the problem of through traffic from the Far East to Western Europe via Soviet Russia.

The conference is attended by representatives of the Soviet Government, France, Germany, Japan, Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania and Poland.

The proposed through route will cover about 8,750 miles and will be the longest in the world. The journey from Tokio to Paris will take a fortnight.

headline: RENNIE'S FOLLY."
text:
MAGIC INCIDENT RECALLED

A GOVERNMENT QUARANTINE STATION.

Rennie's Mills at Junk Bay (or Rennie's Folly as the locality is sometimes known) have been under reconstruction for some time, the work being carried out by the P.W.D., and they are now practically ready for use as a quarantine station.

It was in 1906 that the idea of milling wheat to compete in China with Australian and American flour was put into execution there. The scheme, however, ended in disaster, leading to the suicide of Rennie, the man who had primarily interested himself in it, and to heavy loss by a well-known bank which held mortgages on the property. The reason for the failure of the scheme is difficult to understand as the locality had natural advantages and deep water enabled ships to go practically alongside. But it certainly proved a gigantic failure and Rennie, on whose mind it had preyed, jumped overboard from the launch one day as it was returning to Hongkong.

The mills remained derelict until the Government bought them finally to make use of them as a quarantine station. This will be for the purpose of keeping under observation deck hands from ships on which there has been small-pox or cholera, there being at present no means of keeping in touch with such persons when they leave the ship. Cabin passengers will not be required to go there as it is much easier to keep track of them, and if necessary to make periodical examination for any signs of disease.

Station would be ready for use, the Hon. Dr. J. B. Addison, P.C.M.O., said that, if necessary, it could be brought into use straight away, although the work was not actually quite completed. There would be capacity for almost 2,000, if necessary, as the huge storing rooms of the original mills had been made use of. Its situation was good as it was remote and not easy to get away from. With cholera notified from Swatow it might have to be brought into use at any moment.

headline: THE P. & O. LINE
text:
REVIEW AT ANNUAL MEETING

ECONOMIC QUESTIONS.

Lord Inchcape, presiding at the meeting of the Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co., Ltd., touched on a number of economic questions affecting the Company's interests. He said the replenishment of ships suspended in consequence of the high shipbuilding costs reduced the dividend distribution, which was only made possible by the help of investments and drawing on reserves.

He condemned the Protection- ist policy in the application of the Safeguarding of Industries Act.

Referring to the question of the Dominions tariffs, he drew attention to their disposition to shut out manufactures by tariffs or subsidies, and mentioned in this connection the latest proposal of India to put an Import Duty on British coal, while in the case of Australia, it was concluded from statistics that immigrants were increasingly entering urban industries as against settling on the land, and the former were being more and more protected against imports.

Lord Inchcape said it appeared to be the aim of India and the Dominions to manufacture all their requirements and to import nothing. Therefore Britain could not rely on Empire trade. He declared we could not escape the dependence of foreign markets.

He was convinced that the restoration of the gold standard was proper.

He considered that Trade Unionists would never succumb to the seditious doctrine which had its headquarters at Moscow. He was of the opinion that not ten per cent. of the seamen had at heart the recent strike in Australia and South Africa, which was led by avowed Communists. The significant fact was that only British vessels were involved.

These extremists in Australia were defeated by Mr. S. M. Bruce, "a statesman with both courage and determination."

headline: WEMBLEY RESULTS.
text:
SMALLER SALES BUT IMPERIAL BENEFIT.

HON MR. HALLIFAX BACK.

Until the expenses of restoring the site to its previous condition are known, also the complete result of sales, it is impossible to estimate the whole of the cost of Hongkong's participation in the British Empire Exhibition but the indications are that it will be in the neighbourhood of the estimates on which was based the Government grant.

The proceeds of sales in the Hongkong section were less this year than last, said the Hon. Mr. E. R. Hallifax to a "China Mail" representative this morning but he thought on the whole that the system of Government supervision had proved a success in other ways in comparison with that of private enterprise.

The health of the eighty-four Chinese exhibitors had been exceptionally good owing to the excellent supervision of Dr. Marriott in fact there had been one case of serious illness only. The delegates comprising the Chinese exhibitors had expressed their appreciation of the arrangements made for them on the way there and back; the boats used in each instance were those of the Blue Funnel line.

With regard to the disposal of Hongkong's buildings at Wembley, Mr. Halifax said that it would probably be an expense rather than a source of income. The site had to be restored to its previous condition and it was easily to be understood that with the "enormous area of other similar buildings to be disposed of and their lack of suitability in design for other purposes that this was going to be no easy matter. The Disposals Board were supposed to have something in view and were in negotiations direct with the Government but it is was difficult to see what joint schemes could be evolved.

As regarded the Empire Exhibition generally, Mr. Halifax said that although there had been immediate financial loss for the Association and for the Dominions and Colonies participating, the tone among the overseas representatives was one of optimism as to the ultimate outcome. It seemed to be agreed that value would in due time be shewn for the money expended, large as the sum concerned was — so large indeed that a repetition of the Exhibition on the same scale is hardly to be looked for. It was, however, opportune, and succeeded in the object of lying foundations for sound Imperial building, in the future. Imperial importance was stressed more than it was in 1924—and the Dominions and the Colonies were in a better position after the experience of 1924 to carry out the ideas which had led to their participation originally.

headline: EXPERT
text:
VICKERS LIMITED'S BOLD POLICY.

ENAMPLM TO THE COUNTRY (Routor's Service)

In reaching the decision cabled yesterday, Vickers directors had the advice of Mr. Frank Dudley Docker, Mr. Reginald McKenna, and Sir William Plender, whose recommendations include besides a reconstituted Directorate, the establishment of three management boards, one of which will control the Industrial Section of the business and its subsidiary undertakings; another to control the armaments and ship building side, and a third to be the Finance Board.

These advisers consider the causes of the present situation of Vickers are general trade depression; the depreciation in foreign exchanges; the reduced earning capacity of the company's works which is attributable to the world-reduction in armament expenditure and the home production of armaments by foreign countries; the decline of ship building; foreign competition in the world markets; the financial stringency; and political unrest in Europe which has restricted the giving of credit and retarded schemes of development.

The advisers add that in carrying out after the war the sound policy of changing from swords to ploughshares, the management lacked the special experience required to direct large and varied industrial undertakings.

The advisers at the request of the board have agreed to act in a consultative capacity until the three management boards are working.

The papers congratulate Vickers on the bold reconstruction step which must sooner or later be imitated by other industrial companies if they wish to recover even in a modest degree their past prosperity.

They point out that the present market value of Vickers Ordinary Shares corresponds in the closest degree to "the value which, it is now suggested, should be placed thereon. Therefore little effect will be produced on the market.

headline: A WIFE'S DEBTS.
text:
HUSBAND IS NOT LIABLE.

WHEN A

THE HIND-LAMMERT CASE:

Mr. W. B. Hind's contention that he was not obliged to pay for debts incurred by his wife was upheld yesterday afternoon by Mr. Justice Wood who gave a verdict in his favour in the case in which Lammert Bros. sued for $218 for furniture sold to Mrs. Hind in the sales rooms.

His Honour emphasised that the furniture was delivered to Mrs. Hind at an address other than her own residence for the purpose of furnishing a flat which she proposed to let on her own account. The residence where defendant and his wife were living was already furnished.

The law applicable had been stated by Mr. Justice McCardie in a judgment in 1922: "A person who deals with a married woman on credit does so, as far as regards a remedy, against the husband, at his own risk.

Continuing. His Honour said marriage in itself did not give a wife authority to pledge her husband's credit. A husband might give express authority to his wife or he might give authority by a coarse of cor. by which he implied conferred authority to contract with one or more persons. After any such authority a wife who is living with her husband, from the fact of conabitation, is held to derive a presumptive authority to contract for her husband but that authority is strictly limited.

In the dispute between the parties no question had arisen of express authority or of authority by estoppel. The plaintiffs, therefore, in order to succeed, had to rely on the presumptive authority arising from cohabitation for the wife to pledge her husband's credit for necessaries.

Lastly the fact that the plaintiffs were public auctioneers and announced in their printed conditions of sale "cash on delivery," seemed to him to estop them from setting up any presumptive authority in a married woman who might be a successful bidder at a public auction to pledge her husband's credit.

He therefore gave judgment for the defendant.

Mr. Hind, who appeared yesterday and at the hearing for himself as defendant, said he had already agreed with his friend to pay for the articles in question. He had contested the case purely and simply as a matter of principle.

headline: MEETING A
text:
KOWLOON UNION CHURCH PROGRESS.

ANNUAL MEETING ITEMS:

At the annual meeting of the Kowloon Union Church last night, the Rev. J. Kirk Maconachie (Hongkong pastor) said that today nobody would say they had been ahead of time as it had become more evident that the church was greatly needed.

The Rev. J. Horace Johnston, B.A., presided over a large attendance of the congregation. Mr. C. Wallace, the hon. treasurer, reported an increased balance, viz., $731.74.

Items in the report of the hon secretary, Mr. D. J. Purves were:—

Great advance on attendance at services since 1924.

Many improvements and additions to Church and grounds.

Mr. Andrews replaced Mrs. Craig as organist, & presentation

having been made to the latter. Mr. Fleming took the place of Captain Davies as choirmaster.

In the New Year the minister gave a party to children on his own outlay. A social sub-committee was appointed in January; a gathering was held in March and another in November. Weekly bathing picnics were held till the strike intervene. $85.80 was realised for a crockery account. The committee recommends a monthly social event.

Collections have been most liberal; special thankofferings at the anniversary making up for lean strike months.

Thanks are expressed to Sunday school workers, attendance having increased from 25 to 45.

Five marriages and eight baptisms had been performed and 100 names were on the communion role.

The Rev. Mr. Maconachie presented to the Church a bible purchased at Home.

Officers elected were:—

Ladies—Mrs. J. A. Craig, Mrs. D. Davies, Mrs. Dick, Mrs. D. F. Warren, Mrs. D. M. Nelson, Miss Farrell.

Gentlemen—Messrs. Arnott, D. Gow, J. Cameron, W. McFarlane, D. F. Warren, E. C. Tregilles, J. Smith, D. J. Purves.

headline: WAR IN SOUTH.
text:
PAKHOI NOW IN "RED" "HANDS."

HOIHOW TO FALL NEXT?

Quoting a passenger from that port, the local vernacular papers state that Hoihow is now in the hands of the Canton (Kuomin-tang) army.

An anti-Hongkong boycott has been started and conditions are similar to those prevalent at Swatow. Order has been maintained. Hoihow has not yet been brought into line but the speaker at its position will be the same as that of Pakhol in a few days' time. It is notified that the name of the Dapusta York and Company Limited and The Cooperhouse Trading Association, Trusted have been struck off the Register.

headline: “MURDER” ECHO.
text:
FREEDOM FOR NINE

NORTH POINT FIGHT SEQUEL.

After many weeks in custody, on remand, the nine coolies employed at the North Point Harbour works, who were arrested in connection with the death of a co-worker found beaten to death, were set free this morning.

Two workmen were tied up and attacked and one succumbed. As a result, after a count of murder has been amended, two of the defendants were held on a charge of manslaughter and the other seven on a less serious charge. This morning Mr. E. Lindsell, in discharging the men, said that although he believed they were implicated it was not possible to identify them in the evidence, there being several hundreds of coolies employed.

Det.-Inspector T. Murphy prosecuted for the Crown.

headline: MOTOR DANGERS.
text:
TRAM RUNS INTO A CAR.

M. Eleodoro Rouillon, the Peruvian Consultant in Hongkong, escaped serious injury in a motor accident yesterday evening when the car in which he was seated was bumped in the rear by a tram.

The incident occurred at the junction of Pedder Street and Des Vaux Road Central about 7 p.m. Near the traffic policeman's post the car had drawn and, it is stated, the tram could not be brought up in time. A local resident attributes the crash to a coolie stepping in front of the pointsman at the critical moment.

headline: MATTER OF PRIDE.
text:
TRIBUTE TO VOLUNTEER WORKERS

ST. JOHN AMBULANCE BRIGADE

Having proved their usefulness to the community more than ever this year in attendance on street resident cases, strike work and more particularly at Po Hing Fong where they were the first on the scene and rendered valuable aid the St. John Ambulance Brigade of Hongkong assembled at Government House this morning for the presentation of awards.

Morris, Division Superintendents, Messrs. J. Ralston (Kowloon division) and A. eleArculli (Indian division).

headline: WAGES CLAIM.
text:
EUROPEAN LADY SUED AT KOWLOON.

WITHOUT NOTICE.

DISMISSA1

A Chinese coolie and an amah summoned Mrs. McKim, of Humphrey's Flat, for a month's wages at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning. The evidence was that the defendants were dismissed on November 27 without notice. They were asked to call for their wages later, but on calling the defendant refused to pay.

Defendant claimed to have paid $30 between the two servants whom she engaged during the strike. She informed the servants on November 22 through Mr. Mackintosh's boy that their services would not be required after November 26, and the money was paid the day after the conversation.

The case was adjourned for the boy to be called.

headline: Mr. Ho Kom-tong.
text:
The generosity of Mr. Ho Kom- tong in defraying all the expenses of the Corps has already been mentioned to your Excellency. I may add that we never receive any financial assistance from the Government, nor are we allowed to receive fees or payment of any kind from patients. We propose to hold before the end of the month, the annual competitions for the Brigade efficiency shield and venture to hope that Your Excellency will honour us by being present on the occasion and presenting the shield to the win- ners. By way of relaxation, our members are encouraged to take up various sports; boxing, swimming, cricket and football are popular. One of the events in the swimming contests is a life saving competition in which a dummy of the size and weight of the average man is thrown into the water, recovered and brought ashore by each competitor in turn, and the various methods of the re- suscitation of the apparently drowned, demonstrated.

I now beg to ask you, sir, to dis- tribute the various awards.

Very Smart Appearance.

After distributing the awards His Excellency said that it was a real pleasure for him to renew association with their brigade. "I am particularly glad to note the very smart appearance of those who appear before me to-day," said His Excellency. "I congratulate the recipients of the certificates, and am very pleased to note that a number have renewed them for five and four years, in some cases even longer, also the winners of trophies.

"It is a matter of pride, I think, to the community, that there should be so many volunteers willing to train themselves efficiently to: the good for their fellow citizens in Hongkong. I shall take the keenest interest in your work and I hope to see a great deal more from time to time in the course of the next few months. I accept the invitation of your Commissioner to attend at the display to take place before the end of the month."

"As Head of the Government, also, I am pleased to see so many men in the railway service who have trained themselves to give first aid in cases of accidents. I shall do my utmost to see that before long a very large percentage of officers and men in the police force are similarly trained. I wish you good day and all success throughout the coming year."

headline: SYRIAN BANDIT.
text:
THREAT TO FRENCH COMMISSIONER.

TO CUT OFF HIS HEAD!

In a speech at a banquet in his honour, at Aleppo, M. de Jouvenel, the new French High Commissioner, said Syria was calm except in the districts of Damascus and Jebel Druse, where a minority was warring, not against France but against Syria.

Since his arrival at Aleppo he heard persistent demands for the separation of Aleppo from Damascus.

This was the result of fratricidal war.

Hassan Kharrat, the Moslem bandit leader, operating in the Chagour quarter of Damascus had sent a letter to a local paper stating he had detailed 40 men to cut off M. de Jouvenel's head, adding, "here is our reply to his speeches."

headline: PEACE MOVE.
text:
CANTON MERCHANTS OFFER?

LOAN TO END STRIKE:

"Extras" have been issued by a Canton vernacular paper, says a merchant who arrived here yesterday and was interviewed by a Hongkong Chinese reporter, stating that a large sum of money will be advanced by a Canton merchant—to be ultimately repaid by the Canton Government—to bring about a settlement of the strike and boycott.

After reviewing the steps already taken and the appointment of delegates, the publisher of the "extra" says that he understands that a certain wealthy merchant in Canton is willing to advance this large sum, which will be repaid in due course, after the strike is ended, by the Provincial Government.

Mr. Kan Kum-shek also arrived here yesterday, and stated that he came to ascertain when the Hong-kong "fraternal" party would leave.

Mr. Yeung Sai-ngzaam is expected to return to Canton early this week.

The list of names for inclusion in the party closed yesterday. According to present expectations the party may leave on Thursday or Friday.

Mr. Kan had nothing new to report in connection with the appointment of delegates by Canton.

headline: MOTOR ACCIDENTS.
text:
COOLIE INJURED. FATALLY.

TWO MINOR MISHAPS.

A Chinese earth coolie died at the Kwong Wah Hospital yesterday evening from injuries which he received earlier in the day in a motor accident at Tsun Wan Road.

The driver of the motor car in a statement alleged that the coolie was crossing the road and hesitated in front of his car. The front wheel struck the man down and he fell on his head.

In another accident near the “Star” ferry station yesterday morning, a European lady travelling in a ricsha was thrown out when a motor car coming behind collided with the vehicle and overturned it. The lady escaped injury, but the ricsha was slightly damaged.

On Saturday afternoon a Chinese girl received slight bruises when a motor car knocked her down at Queen's Road East near the Wanchai Market.

headline: "ANTI-FOREIGN."
text:
STRANGE REPORT FROM CANTON

DEMONSTRATION TO-MORROW?

Moves to organise an anti-Christian and anti-foreign demonstration in Canton to-morrow are said to be disfavoured by the Provinciall Government.

The demonstration, or procession—about which word has reached the Canton authorities—may be the predecessor of something promised for Christmas for which a certain section had planned things on a fairly extensive scale.

It may also be that the preparations for to-morrow—and there certainly have been signs that the organisation is ready—may be more anti-Christian, essentially, than anti-foreign.

At any rate the Canton Government is rumoured to be striving to restrict the demonstrators to the city which is taken to mean giving the Shakee and adjacent parts of the Bund a wide berth.

Some of the more conservative of the Kuomintang politicians are even said to be opposed to the idea of a procession along the waterfront, this report emanating from a statement that steps have been taken to be ready for emergencies.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE. / BIG CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.
text:
FORTHCOMING LEGAL BATTLE

Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen have applied for writs claiming £20,000 each from the Government alleging wrongful arrest and imprisonment.

Mrs. Walsh and Mrs. Johannsen are also claiming £5,000 for loss of their husbands' services.

It may be recalled that Mrs Walsh was formerly Miss Adela Pankhurst, the militant. suf-fragette.

This is an echo of the recent seamen's strike in Australia when the Government felt compelled to use drastic measures of arrest, imprisonment and deportation. Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen were arrested, but subsequently released on an order of the Supreme Court of Australia, and are now claiming against the Government.

Mrs. Walsh, was formerly Miss Adela Pankhurst, of the Pankhurst trio who led the suffragette movement some years ago. When the movement succeeded, the Pankhurst family withdrew from it. The other sister is engaged in religious work.

headline: INDIA'S CONDITION. / VICEROY'S "ROSY PICTURE."
text:
COMMERCIAL ENERGY.

A rosy picture of India's economic condition was painted by Lord Reading in an exhaustive address to the Indian Chambers of Commerce.

He recalled the depressing conditions of 1921 and the adverse trade balance, 800,000,000 rupees. The political atmosphere was

headline: £3,000,000 LOAN. / HONGKONG AND THE BOYCOTT.
text:
FURTHER ASSISTANCE POSSIBLE

In the House of Commons, Mr. A. Spoor asked for information of the purposes of the loan of £3,000,000 to the Hongkong Government; and whether the Government had taken steps to terminate the boycott of British trade in Hongkong.

Mr. Ormsby Gore replied that the Governor had applied in September for a loan of the amount mentioned for the purpose of restoring confidence and financing trade.

· The loan had saved the Colony at a serious moment.

It is possible that if the boycott continues and trade worsens, further assistance may have to be considered next year.

headline: A STOLEN BANGLE. / SUSPICION LEADS TO ARREST.
text:
A HEAVY SENTENCE

Sentience of six months $ ^{1} $ hard labour and 15 strokes of the birch was imposed by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on a Chinese charged with larceny of a gold-mounted bangle from a little girl.

The complainant, a Chinese married woman, stated in evidence that she was at a market stall in Eastern Street yesterday afternoon along with her family of three small children. Defendant was observed to be petting one of the girls, whom he enticed some distance away, when he stole the bangle. The theft was noticed when the girl came back to the complainant, but the defendant had then disappeared.

The suspicions of a Chinese detective were aroused when he met a man on the pavement who suddenly stopped in his walk, stared at him, and walked again. A little further down the road the detective was informed of the theft, and in a search the "suspect" was caught in a side street. The stolen bangle was found in his pocket. These facts were given by the detective in his evidence.

His Worship imposed sentence as stated above.

headline: THE BOYCOTT.
text:
EDWARD

WHAMYOA AND HONGKONG.

Sir Edward Stubs, ex-Gover- er of Hongkong, was the guest of the Colonial Institute at a City luncheon at which no em- phasised that the troubles of Hongkong were started by Rass- in a legislators at Canton who made no self-retest of their intention to rain Hongkong.

Sir E. Stubbs contended that his counter-strike methods were not unpopular amongst those they were meant to protect. He did not think the trouble would last much longer.

He had great faith in the commonsense of the Kwangtung Chinese, who, before long, would purify Canton of the "Red" element.

When the situation was normal, Hongkong would have a future far exceeding the past. There was no possibility of Hongkong being cut out by any other part. The Cantonese were talking wildly of developing Whampoa, which, however, would require much dredging, whilst there were other drawings.

Tho really important question was the completion of the will way from Canton to Hanking. He feared that the late Dr. Sun Yat Sen. misunderstood him during the recent abortive negotiations on finance in connection with the Canton line from Hongkong.

headline: THAT NEW PORT. / LOWER THAN WHAMPOA FAVOURED? RIVER HEAL SCHEME
text:
“A certain gentleman who comes from Canton” is quoted by the vernacular papers of this morning, as having expounded a project by the Provincial Government to organise a big port at the mouth of the Canton River, further down than Whampoa.

At first, so the speaker is reported, the Kwangtung Government considered the Bak Ngo Taam (that part of the Canton Harbour by Shameen and leading to the "back reach") the widest anchorage. It was the intention to accommodate bigger ships at Whampoa but the water there has been found to be too shallow. Accordingly, a project is being mooted to develop the port of Tai Ping (at the head of the estuary and close to Bocca Tigris) and its suburb of Sha Kok (sometimes known as the Sha Kok Fort).

headline: STRIKE EXAMINATION
text: The Canton Admiralty has despatched the "Kong Hon" to patrol the Bocca Tigris Passage to examine incoming foreign vessels. It having been reported to the Strike Executive that merchandise is being shipped to Canton from Shanghai under changed labels special examination pickets have been added.

headline: BACK IN COLONY.
text:
A RETURNED BANISHEE'S DOINGS.

SENTENCES TO FIT THE CRIME.

Attempting to extort money by posing as a police constable and returning from banishment were charges against a Chinese brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

The evidence was that a man was arrested on Sunday on a charge of being concerned in a Triad Society. Defendant, representing himself to be a constable, visited the man's home the following day and demanded $6 from his wife, stating that he would put in a good word with the police on behalf of her husband. Defendant was asked to call again for the money. The next day the husband was released and on hearing from his wife about the visitor's demand a trap was laid with the assistance of the police. When arrested he was recognised as a banisher.

Defendant was sentenced to three months hard labour for posing as a constable, and one year's hard labour for returning from banishment. In addition he was ordered to receive 15 strokes of the birch.

headline: WAGES CLAIM
text:
KOWLOON.SUMMONS DISMISSED:

SERVANTS FAIL TO APPEAR.

The summons against Mrs. McKim, of Humphreys Flate, Kowloon, for recovery of a month's wages for alleged dismissal without notice of a house coolie and amah failed at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning.

The case was adjourned from Monday for the evidence of a house boy to be taken, but the failure of the complainants to appear in Court to-day resulted in the summons being dismissed.

DRIVER CHARGED WITH MANSLAUGHTER.

SUNDAY'S MOTOR ACCIDENT.

As a sequel to the death of a Chinese earth coolie from injuries received in an accident on the Tsun Wan Road on Sunday, a motor driver of the Yau Lok garage was charged before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning.

headline: LOCAL DISTRAINTS
text:
WHEN THEY ARE NOT

A BAILIFF'S DUTY.

Having fallen into arrears with rent payment a distress was, and was issued against a Chinese master of a river steamer and the balliff visited the address, 107, Wing Lok Street, which was given as that of the man who owed the money. Here he seized furniture and trade goods which it subsequently transpired were U.S. property of firms to whom the man in question had sub-let. An application was therefore made for wrongful distress and Mr. Justice Wood gave his yerdict today.

He pointed out that according to the law at Home, it was legal to seize all chattels which were on the tenants' premises without reference to ownership but quoted the local Ordinance under which property can only be seized which is found in the house and in the "apparent" possession of the person from whom the rent is claimed.

As the tenant in question in this case was in seafaring man and the goods in question were not those which one would expect to find in the possession of a man of that type, also, taking into consideration that the goods were stated at the time to the bailiff to be other than those of the tenant owing money, his Honour found that deress had been wrongfully levied. The property seized was prior to be released. Each party was to pay costs of action. Mr. O. A. S. Russ represented the successful claimant and Mr. H. A. Wade in the owner of the property.

A Government spokesman has stated that Chang Tso-lin and Kuo Sung-ling will be notified by the Japanese that no fighting will be permitted within six miles of the capital.

The spokesman stated that all Consuls have requested Japan to take all steps to protect foreigners in the capital.

Japanese troops have been in- stricted to maintain absolute neutrality.

No more troops are to be sent except the aforementioned, unless the situation demands it.

It is explained that the Portsmouth treaty allowed Japan approximately 15,000 railway guards in Manchuria, but even with reinforcements the total is only 8,000.

The Japanese do not expect that Chang Tso-lin will attempt refuge in Mukden, even as a private citizen, as his life is endangered by the Chinese; but will probably feel to Dairen or some other Japanese territory, if defeated.

headline: A HUNGRY THIEF.
text:

CYCLE PAWNED FOR FOOD.

Stealing a motor cycle belonging to Mr. P. Vickers while he was on a visit at a friend's house at Cameron Road, Kowloon, on Xmas Day, a Chinese left the machine by way of security for a meal he had taken at a restaurant. No sooner had the machine been restored to its owner by the efforts of the Police than it was spirited away again the following morning from outside Cambay Buildings. Trying the same dodge at another restaurant, the thief was caught.

These facts were given in evidence when the man was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning on four charges of theft and obtaining meals with intent to defraud.

Defendant, who pleaded guilty to the latter charges, was sentenced to four months hard labour altogether.

headline: BOOK ENTRIES.
text:
DISCREPANCIES IN CASHIER'S RECORD.

COUNSEL SUGGESTS UNTRUTH. FULNESS.

Mr. Chau, the compradone of Gertz Bros. Co. (of the Orient), Ltd., was cross-examined at considerable length this morning by Mr. Zeitlyn (for the defence) with regard to entries in the cashier's books respecting the items in regard to which the Crown alleges misappropriation against Mr. James Edward Atherley, former manager. In the course of his cross-examination, Mr. Zeitlyn put it to the compradone that his books were untrue but this was denied. Some mistakes might have crept in, the witness admitted, but they would have been corrected. The witness was taken over carefully each item entered on the relevant days in three books, one a record in English, one a record in Chinese and another a book, which were recorded promissory note numbers by which payments into the bank were checked.

When these items had all been gone over (a proceeding which took well over an hour) His Lordship commented to the jury that there were several things in the Chinese version which were not in the English version. Reference to payments into the bank do not appear in the English version which do in the Chinese. Mr. Zeiflyn: Furthermore, the English version gives payments into the bank on dates of receipt whereas the Chinese version gives them on a different date.

These discrepancies were then pointed out to the witness and he was asked for his explanation. With regard to an entry in one version in which payment into the bank was stated to have been made on March 22 whereas in the "other it was" stated to be March 25, witness said he thought the explanation was that Mr. Atherley had asked the cashier for that amount on that day. Mr. Atherley then might have given him a receipt and the man who wrote the book might not know what would have happened. The cashier would consider his responsibility at an end once the money was handed to the "taipan." When Mr. Atherley returned the money the chop was put on in the other book for that date.

Mr. Zeitlyn reminded witness of the clause in his contract under which he was liable to be called upon to make a true statement of the accounts in his charge. Had he discharged his obligation when no reference to this money lent to the "talpan" appeared in the book?

An alteration in the book of the date of paying in to the bank of money received from Tsun Tsaun Chun was referred to Mr. Zeitlyn. Why had this been altered to March 27 he asked. "Witness admitted that there was an alteration but said that he could not account for it. It was a matter for the cashier to explain.

Mr. Zeitlyn suggested that it had been "made to fit."

The entering up in respect to money received, as having been paid into the Asia Banking Corporation was also pointed out by Mr. Zeitlyn.

Witness admitted that the company had no dealings with that bank. He thought it must have been a clerical error.

Mr. Zeitlyn: It makes a great difference to employers, does it not, whether an amount of money collected for them is paid into a bank with which they have an account or into one with which they have no account.

The cross-examination of this witness was not complete when the court adjourned for the tiffin interval.

The interview between Mr. Atherley, a representative of the firm of Getz Bros. and other interested parties, after enquiry into the alleged misappropriations, was detailed at yesterday's hearing. The compradore of Getz Bros., who was under examination by Mr. Zeitlyn at the time stated that he did not hear Mr. Atherley's opinion, that the whole affair was a personal matter between him and the compradore. He admitted that he (witness) asked Mr. Atherley about money.

headline: “GUILTY.”
text:
VERDICT AGAINST SIR BASIL THOMSON

AN APPEAL NOTIFIED:

On the resumption of the case against Sir Basil Thomson, who yesterday pleaded not guilty, Sir Henry Curtis-Bennett, cross-examining the Police witnesses suggested that accused gave his own name "Hume". Thomson, which the Sergeant mistook for "Hugh" Thomson. The Magistrate (Mr. H. L. Cancellor) remarked that that was a mistake which might easily be made.

Mr. Curtis-Bennett, in his speech, said that a man with the knowledge of accused must have been insane or drunk to go to such a place for such an offence. The evidence showed that he was absolutely sober. Counsel was glad that the Magistrate had last night personally inspected the spot and asked the Magistrate to say that it was impossible to see what people were doing from the place where the Police said they saw them. He submitted that the story of the two constables in this connection was untrue.

Mr. Reginald McKenna, and Sir Reginald Ball, M.P., testified to accused's high character, after which accused entered the witness box. He said that since his retirement he had devoted himself to literary and journalistic work, particularly criminal and police matters. He had recently contemplated investigating and writing about Hyde Park and West End solicitation. He had discussed the matter with Mr. Douglas Straight, ex-Inspector-General of Police in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and with Mr. Barry Higgins, the well-known solicitor. He was also very keenly interested in the Communist movement. He went to Hyde Park to investigate the conditions there. A woman spoke to him and told him that she was hard up. He gave her two or three shillings and asked her about the people who were sitting round. Immediately afterward the Police appeared. Accused emphatically denied that the woman was acting improperly toward him.

Incident In Court.

Sir Basil Thomson denied that he said after his arrest "How can I keep this from my friends?" He said that what he did say was that such a charge would ruin anybody.

Counsel for the defence called attention to Laurie (the policeman who arrested Sir Basil Thomson) standing close to the witness box and grimacing whilst the questions were being put.

The Magistrate ordered Laurie to leave the Court.

Sir Basil Thomson denied that he said to Laurie that if he overlooked this he could leave the police to-morrow. He swore that there was not the shadow of foundation for the charge.

The second summons was dismissed.

Sir Basil Thomson was found guilty on the first charge and fined £5 and £5 costs.

An appeal was notined. headline: HEAVY LOANS.
text:
MR. ATHERLEY AND HIS COMPRADORE.

A PERSONAL MATTER?

ADVANCESSAND TO BE COMPANY MONEYS.

For the fourth day, the cross-examination of Mr. Chau,� compradore of Former Getz Bros. Co. (of the Orient Ltd.) continued at the Criminal Sessions proceedings this morning in the case in which Mr. J. E. Atherley is charged with misappropriation.

The issues between the prosecution and the defence were put early to the jury this morning by the Chief Justice.

The Crown says that Mr. Atherley took company money and raised it for his own purposes. Mr. Atherley says, on the other hand that he got these moneys from the compradore (he did not care where the compradore got them) but treated them as a long from the compradore. He treated them as the moneys of the compradore.

Mr. F. C. Jenkin (for the Crown) concurred and Mr. Zeithyn said that he wished he could have put the case as fairly.

A complaint which Mr. Atherley had had from head office in California, with regard to extensions of certain drafts beyond their due date was referred to by Mr. Zeitlyn and Mr. Chau, the compradore, was asked whether it was not a fact that Mr. Atherley talked to him about it.

Witness said he had no recollection of it but at about that time Mr. Atherley asked him about amounts outstanding and from an investigation of the books witness told Mr. Atherley they totalled $70,000. Witness reminded Mr. Atherley that $18,000 of this was money lent to him. Mr. Atherley told him to press for quick payment in respect of the balance.

Witness was cross-examined with regard to what Mr. Zeitlyn termed a change of staff about that time, one of the employees leaving about that time. Witness maintained that there had been no change until the name of the former cashier, Cheung Ho-shi, was put to him. This man had not been dismissed, he said, but had changed from cashier to number two compradore in order that witness, who was poorly at that time, might have assistance.

Witness denied that the cashier left that position because he was $10,000 short in his accounts. He also denied that he told Mr. Atherley any of the office staff were short in their accounts. headline: Bank Subpena.

At this stage, Mr. Zeitlyn initiated to His Lordship that he made an application that the International Banking Corporation should be called upon to produce the deposit slips of Mr. Atherley's account, the counterfoils of his paying-in book.

His Lordship intimated that the counterfoils did not come under the heading of “bankers books” mentioned in the particular section of the Ordinance referred to. It was a banker's document and he thought the correct thing to do was for Mr. Zeitlyn to subpoena the Bank.

Mr. Zeitlyn agreed and gave it as his case that ever since the arrest of Mr. Atherley on the morning of October 23 in the Hongkong Hotel, the document in question had been in the compradore department of the firm. This had been denied by the compradore.

Mr. Jenkin then re-examined the compradore and indicated that had he been given any idea of the defence he would have made a longer opening and have brought out facts which he would now have to elicit in re-examination.

Mr. Jenkin reminded witness of the interview which took place between Mr. Atherley, Mr. Parkhurst, the Shanghai manager, and Mr. Kelly, of Head Office, California, when the alleged misappropriations were being enquired into. Mr. Parkhurst and Mr. Atherley had gone out to try,

the complainant in the course of which he said that the second defendant and four others took him to task for not joining the strikers and demanded a sum of $100 as "forgiveness" money. He had paid over $5 on December 4 and a further $5 a fortnight later, it being agreed that the balance would be paid on January 1. In his dilemma he applied to the compradore for a loan of $50, which he intended to pay over with his month's wages amounting to $40. The compradore, on learning the reason why complainant required the money, reported the matter to Mr. J. P. Bourne, the Hotels Superintendent, and the police were notified.

Further evidence was given that a trap was laid by the police and the two defendants were arrested at the meeting place in a tea-house at Staunton Street on Tuesday afternoon when it had been arranged to pay over $10 as a further installment. Two five dollar notes which changed hands had been marked by the police.

In statements made by the defendants, the first denied knowledge of the affair. He said that he went to have tea at the invitation of the second defendant, a clansman of his, and that the complainant was not known to him. The second defendant, who was a recently engaged worker at the Hotel, claimed that he asked the complainant for a loan of $10, as, owing to the fire, no wages had yet been paid. The complainant invited him to have tea first, and he went to the tea-house together with his clansman. The money was handed to him and soon after he was arrested by detectives who were seated at the tables.

The case was adjourned until Monday.

headline: INTIMIDATION.
text:
HOTEL PANTRY BOY'S STORY.

TWO CHINESE CHARGED.

A pantry boy employed at the Hongkong Hotel and who remained at his post throughout the strike was the complainant in a case at the Central Magistracy this morning in which two Chinese were charged with alleged intimidation.

headline: HARBOUR MISHAPS.
text:
STAR" FERRY BUMPS LAUNCH

CARCO JUNK CAPSIZES.

Shortly before 11 last night, the “Morning Star” bumped a Taikoo Dock launch, striking the latter on her port quarter.

This took place near the Hong- kong wharf of the "Star" Ferry. Co. In his report to the Harbour Office, the ferry coxswain makes certain claims as to his steering, being on the quivive, etc.

Two women and four men were thrown into the harbour on Tuesday afternoon and were rescued by a passing Police launch. They were the crew of a cargo junk which was making for a P. & O. steamer at the Kowloon Godowns. A strong blow and the wash from a passing steamer is believed to have caused the capsize.

headline: COAL STRIKE?
text:
STRONG REVULSION OF FEELING.

MOVE BY PUBLISHERS.

The strong revulsion feeling against a coal strike is indicated in a telegram from the publishers of the leading newspapers in the anthracite region to the mine owners' and miners' representatives, who have reached a deadlock at the conference here.

The telegram calls attention to the colossal financial loss, paralysis of business, loss of market for hard coal; and heart-breaking distress that would be caused among the miners.

It adds that the parties' differences regarding arbitration do not justify further division, and the public shall hold the leaders on both sides responsible for the misfortunes of everybody concerned.

headline: STOLEN GOODS.
text:
CONSTABLE SENT TO JAM

© EVIDENCE OF LARCUENY.

A Chinese constable was changed before Mr. R. E. LindseLL at the Central Magistracy this morning with larceny and alternatively with receiving stolen property.

At the previous hearing, the complainant, Mr. William Allen, said that he lost an overcont, a gold watch and a chain, and a sum of money, while on his way home from a dinner. The missing articles, including $22 in bank notes, were found by Detective Sergeant O'Donovan in a room occupied by the defendant at Queen's Road East.

In a long statement the defendant said that he met an old friend whom he invited to his cubicle that night. They had some Chinese wine together and the friend got drunk. Later the visitor went away, leaving the overcoat and a watch and chain in defendant's charge. Defendant called his wife as a witness, and certain portions of his statement were borne out by the woman. Mr. W. R. Scott (A.S.P.) said that the defendant had served for eleven months and had a good record.

The Magistrate held that there was not sufficient evidence to conflict on the charge of larceny. He convicted on the charge of receiving stolen property, the sentence being six months' hard labour.

headline: OPIUM SEIZURES.
text:
CHINESE PASSENGER FINED $2,000.

SMALL HAUL ON A SHIP.

An order was made by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning for confiscation of 35 taels of opium found on board the s.a. "Tenyo Maru." The evidence of an Indian guard was that he found the opium wrapped in a coat and dumped in the lavatory.

On a charge of unlawful possession of 18 taels of opium, a Chinese was fined $2,000 or eight months' hard labour in default. The opium was found concealed under the clothing when the man was searched at the Wing Lok wharf on his way from Macao.

headline: NEGLIGENT ACT. / PANTRY BOY. AND A MOTOR CAR.
text:
TAMPERING WITH GEARS.

An amended charge of negligently damaging a tram car was preferred, this morning against the pantry boy who was before the Central Magistrate yesterday on a charge of driving a motor car without a licence.

After new evidence it was found that the defendant had wilfully turned the switch on and worked the self-starter.

Defendant was fined $10, or fourteen days, and no order was made for compensation to the Tramway Company, as His Worship was informed that Mr. Harry Kong, the owner of the motor car, had already paid $25.

headline: TRUCULENT YOUTH. / ARMS HIMSELF WITH A HATCHET.
text:
A TEA HOUSE DISPUTE.

A Chinese youth was fined $10, or fourteen days' hard labour, and he was further asked to furnish a bond in a surety of $50 to be of good behaviour, when he was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with disorderly conduct at a Chinese tea-house.

Evidence was given that the defendant had a dispute with a waitress and had to be turned out. He came later with a hatchet and threatened to do harm to the inmates. The master of the teahouse blew a police whistle and the youth was arrested.

headline: COAL INDUSTRY.
text:
NO ROYAL ROAD TO ITS RECOVERY

MINERS WHO SLACK!

A demand for the restoration of the eight-hour day in mines was the chief point in the evidence submitted to the Coal Commission on behalf of the owners, who declared that the standards of living must rest on a stable and economic conditions, whilst savings could also be effected and earnings could be increased if the miners attended their work with greater regularity. It was pointed out that absenteeism in Scotland averages 3½ per cent. in England and Wales 8¼ per cent.

The owners expressed their willingness to meet the miners with the utmost goodwill, but they were opposed to the establishment of compulsory machinery for the settlement of disputes. They were unable to point to any royal road for the recovery of the industry, but were confident that lower costs of production would stimulate an already growing demand for British coal.

headline: Continental Hours.
text:
The Chairman declared that if the Mining Association's proposals were accepted the British miners would be working longer than French, Belgian, and German miners.

Cause of Unrest.

Mr. Evan Williams replied that their wages would be considerably higher. He asserted that the unrest in the industry was not spontaneous, but was the result of a deliberate attempt by the miners' leaders to prevent the reconstruction of the industry by private enterprise after decontrol.

text: A memorandum from the Mining Association, which was submitted prior to the taking of evidence, said that if the railway wages bill were reduced all rates for mineral goods traffic could be reduced by 25 per cent.

headline: U. S. STRIKE.
text:
The conference between the employers and the representatives of the strikers in the anthracite coal mines was adjourned without a settlement and without a date for the renewal of the negotiations being determined.

The mine owners insisted upon complete arbitration, whilst the miners maintained that arbitration was only acceptable on the basis of increased wages without any reductions.

It is announced from Wilkes-barre (Pennsylvania) that the Grievance Committee of the Pennsylvania Coal Company today decided to launch a movement to call out all anthracite mine maintenance men for the purpose of forcing the issue and it is generally believed there that the strikers will make a determined effort to tie up the mines completely.

headline: “UNFORTUNATE.”
text:
HIS LORDSHIP ON EARLY DEFENCE.

THE ATHERLEY CASE.

TENTH AND LAST DAYS "HARKING"

At this, the tenth and last day of hearing of the charges of misappropriation of company moneys against James Edward Atherley, former manager of Getz Bros. (of the Orient) Ltd., His Lordship referred to the reservation of defence of Mr. Atherley at the early police court proceedings. In the course of the case, said His Lordship, a statement was made by counsel for the prosecution and also by counsel for the defence as to the fact that in this case accused had had more than one opportunity of making an answer to the charge and had not availed himself of that opportunity. Mr. Zeitlyn had protested that whether accused should or should not have made an answer or given any idea of what his defence might be was a matter wholly for the accused and his representatives.

I fully agree with Mr. Zeitlyn said His Lordship. But, gentlemen (addressing the jury). I sometimes think that gentlemen who appear before us like the accused do not recognise the advantage of a statement made by an accused person as the earliest available opportunity. For instance, supposing when the accused is charged he gives an explanation and you find that the defence which has been adumbrated in his explanation is the defence adopted at the trial, a very strong argument can be based upon that statement. It can be said that his defence has been consistent all along; that at the first available opportunity he stated what his defence was going to be; that all he stated in the witness box is to be believed and the facts as he stated are to be corroborated by the statement originally made by him. Now, take this case as an illustration. Supposing immediately he had had an opportunity the accused had said "it is true that I received these moneys but they were loaned to me by the compradoge. I did not take them knowing them to be the moneys of my employers and treated them as belonging to the compradoge" I think you will see at once how greatly strengthened the defence put up afterwards on behalf of the accused would have been.

However, as I have said, it is a matter solely for the expression of the accused and his advisers and the most you can say in a case where there has been complete reservation of the defence until the case comes on for trial in this court is that it is unfortunate that a statement was not made at once because any defence put up afterwards would have been greatly strengthened by a clear statement of what the defence was at the first available opportunity.

His Lordship then proceeded to sum up and was still summing up when this edition went to press.

Final Speeches.

In the final speech for the defence yesterday, Mr. Zeitlyn emphasised that Mr. Atherley had persisted in statements which demanded a large measure of credulity. When a man did not accept an explanation which would be better for him, and persisted in a statement which was harder to believe, was it not better to believe in a man. For the purposes of the defence it would be the easiest way to put it that moneys advanced by the compradore to Atherley were moneys from the Company. Atherley would not take that view of it. He persisted with determination that the true aspect of the case was that the compradore came to him with L.O.U.'s and O.K.'d bills and these together made a total for which he drew a cheque and handed it to the compradore. Continuing Mr. Zeitlyn said they had seen the compradore in the box. He was a man of considerable williness; he was not a gullible person but one who would not readily assent unless the truth was forced out of him. They would recollect that he (Counsel) had questioned him on five or six occasions about the officers of Getz

Bros. He had asked him what was the position of Mr. Kelly, and he had said he did not know. They would consider the mentality of such a man. And considering that, was it not probable that the story told by accused was the correct one? Was it not easy to believe that the compadore had taken the moneys of the Company as his own? And when moneys were paid back was it not probable that he took O.K.'d "bills and I.O.U's which totalled the sum handed over to Atherley? Surely that was not an improbable explanation. In the light of the character of the man in the box, this true explanation could well carry more confidence in the minds of the gentlemen of the jury for that reason.

Were They Loans?

Proceeding, Mr. Zeitlyn said that there was positive evidence that the transaction between Atherley and the compradore was in the nature of loans. He would deal with them under three heads—handwriting evidence, verbal admission and written evidence. Was it not strange that throughout all the books there was not one entry, showing that payment had been made to Atherley on behalf of Getz Bros.? Outside that exhibit D, there was not a single document, not a single book, not a single line which would show any payment to Atherley on behalf of the Company. They would recollect that their foreman had asked the compradore why there was no entry, and he had replied that having handed the moneys over to Atherley, he had finished with the matter. Then there was the compradore's admission. He (Counsel) could not conceive of anything of greater support to the defence than an admission made by the compradore, that he looked to Atherley for repayment of the money which he had advanced to him. And there was even a stronger admission. He had said, "I had it always in mind to turn these I.O.U.'s and bills against the Company, if Atherley did not pay." And they would remember that a very wary, "wily man had made that answer.

Prosecution's Case.

Mr. Jenkin, Counsel for the prosecution, said that the true solution was whether Atherley knew in fact that moneys of the Company were going into his account, and in refunding cheques did he know he was refunding them to the Company. He (Counsel) held that he did know, and his learned friend had tried to get out of it by bringing in suggestions of fraud.

Having regard to Atherley's evidence entirely, he submitted that it was an affront to the intelligence of six men to ask them to believe that from start to finish, he did not know where the moneys came from, nor the true purpose for which every cheque was drawn by him. A deposit slip for May 28 showed that the totals collected were exactly the amount of a cheque drawn by Atherley. That was for the purpose of refunding moneys he had previously taken. They would remember those examples of intricate calculations, and Atherley would have them believe, that he did not know what they were for. Can you believe that this man, of whose probity and integrity, so much has been made, is telling you the truth?

Dealing with Mr. Atherley's banking account, Mr. Jenkin asked whether it was a coincidence that into this "most peculiar account for a man on this man's salary," money was poured at a rate which made even members practising at the Bar envious? Was it a coincidence that the account was opened on Settlement Day—on the eve prior to the day when he had to pay over certain sums? Was it a coincidence that on this day the Company's money went into this account, and not into the Company's account? Was there any necessity for Mr. Atherley to take a wad of the Company's shares and put it into this other account? In his own judgment, he had considered that the circumstances of this case were so strong that he did not wish to weary them with several details.

headline: DISARMAMENT.
text:
SOVIET ACCEPTS LEAGUE'S INVITATION.

AN IMPORTANT CONDITION.

The official Tass Agency learns authoritatively that the Soviet has decided to accept the invitation of the League of Nations to participate in the preliminary Disarmament Conference, and will not object to the participation of Soviet experts in the preliminary Commission on Economic Subjects, provided that these Commissions do not meet, on Swiss territory.

It is a fact that four delegates have been selected to make representations to the authorities concerned for permission to in-augurate a period of unrestricted travelling. Whether the mission will leave just yet remains to be decided.

headline: MURDERS OF COMMUNIST OFFICIALS.
text:
AUTHORITIES QUIESCENT.

It is reported that much unrest prevails among the peasantry in various parts of Soviet Russia and particularly in Ukraine, White-Russia, where armed anti-Bolsheviks are active.

Murders of over-zealous. Communist officials are reported, chiefly in the Bobruisk district, where the militia and the local authorities are alleged to have refused to act against the rebels and are even co-operating with them.

headline: TREATY BETWEEN SWEDEN AND DENMARK.
text:
The new Swedo-Danish Arbitration Treaty has been concluded. It is similar in character to the recent Swedo-Norwegian Convention, and prohibits the employment of armed force for the settlement of disputes.

The Treaty will operate for twenty years, and be"renewable unless two years' notice is given.

headline: “BRASS HATS.”
text:
Some Colonial authorities have a weird respect for "the great W. broad arrow D. which, we hope, will not extend to the R.N. in this Colony, remarks the "Topicist" in the "Singapore Free Press." The War Office has "presented" to Hongkong the sites of two batteries (now of course obsolete) for the purposes of Hongkong University. Whereupon the Legislative Council were asked to express its "deep appreciation of this generous gift." We suppose that Hongkong is so little used to getting anything of its own back out of the great Brass Hats, that it has lost its sense of realities. The land was the Colony's, lent to the W.D. for a mutually advantageous purpose, to revert to the Colony when that purpose was no longer fulfilled. The Topicist hopes that a reversion clause is inserted in this Colony's grants of land for military purposes. One of these days we shall want the lite of Tanglin Barracks for a new Government House, and perhaps the site of Normanton for residences for Municipal employees.

headline: IMPUDENT ROBBERY
text:
HOUSE OPPOSITE POLICE STATION.

FIVE YEARS AND THE "CAT."

Five years' imprisonment with hard labour and twelve strokes of the "cat" was the sentence on a Chinese who was found guilty at the Criminal Sessions this morning of having effected an entry into a house in Eastern Street in his capacity of chicken dealer and then to have attempted assault and robbery.

The audacity of the attempt was commented upon by Mr. Justice Wood in view of the fact that it took place on the top floor of the house immediately opposite No. 7 Police Station.

The prisoner had sold chickens at the house before, and therefore effected entry easily. A knock was heard shortly after he arrived and prisoner said: "That is all right, that is my foki." The latter was admitted, whereupon the prisoner seized one of the woman occupants and the other man the other. The younger of the two women broke away from her assailant, however, and gave the alarm, whereupon both men decamped and got clear away at the time. The arrest followed later and both women identified the prisoner as the man in question. Two knives found on the stairs down, which the men had run were similar to those used by cooked fowl vendors, said Inspector Grant in the course of his evidence.

Evidence was given that the prisoner had brought out a knife similar to the ones left behind and in the course of the struggle with one of the women she had been wounded her in the hand and forearm.

headline: OPIUM CHARGE.
text:
SON USED TO CARRY THE DRUG.

OLD OFFENDER CONVICTED:

A small boy was caught by an Indian constable at Shaukiwan with a small quantity of opium. On information given by the boy it was found that he had been used by his father as a carrier, and the latter was arrested.

When the elder man was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession, Mr. F. G. Vaux pleaded in defence that the opium was used as medicine. His Worship agreed that opium was medicine, but drew attention to the fact that defendant had two previous convictions in 1923 under the Opium Ordinance. A fine of $100, or six weeks' hard labour was imposed.

headline: TOWN SHELLED.
text:
MERCHANTS FIGHT STRIKE PICKETS.

GUNBOAT $ \underline{\text{OPENS}} $ FIRE.

Pakkai (Kongmoon), Jan. 8. Shells were dropped on Muk Chow on January 3 and a few shops were burned following a brush between merchants and strike pickets.

The pickets reached Muk Chow on the gunboat "Kung Hon" and started to examine goods imported. At first the natives raised opposition. Troubles soon broke out and the civilians fled when the warship opened fire.

About three hundred pickets arrived here from Canton on January 8. Sixty remained and the rest moved on to Kongmoon, Kwonghoi, etc.

News has come down that an anti-Christian demonstration has taken place at Sanwui city where posters have been freely distributed and posted conspicuously on walls.

On January 4 a fire broke out on the Hongkong-Kongmoon steamer "Kung On". At the beginning of the strike the vessel was tied up. In August she was removed to her owner's village, Kongmei. Subsequently she was taken to Taiping town. The stamer suffered considerable damage from fire. A few junks carrying firewood were also involved and a good many shops on shore also caught fire.

headline: CONTRABAND.
text:
LOTTERY TICKETS IN AN ENVELOPE.

AN UNSATISFACTORY PLEA.

In a case of unlawful possession of Po Piu lottery tickets at the Central Magistracy this morning, a Chinese told Mr. R. E. Lindsell that he was given 50 cents to carry the tickets for another man who was following behind. His Worship expressed surprise that he should receive such a sum for the work of merely carrying an envelope containing the lottery tickets and said he must have known that it contained contraband. Defendant pleaded he did not know. A line of $50, or four weeks hard labour was imposed.

headline: OFFICIAL SILENCE.
text:
ITALY'S DEBT BEING DISCUSSED.

CLEARING THE GROUND

The Italian debt negotiations are proceeding enshrouded in official silence which is only occasionally broken for the issue of denials to the circumstantial stories published from time to time.

It is stated that the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Winston Churchill wants a settlement concluded early in the coming week.

If this is true the negotiations will have to be speeded up considerably, as it is understood that agreement has not yet been reached regarding the amount at which the debt is to be placed for the purposes of negotiation, though the experts were busy over the week-end discussing the technical details.

headline: HABITUAL THIEF.
text:
CONVICTED AGAIN AT KOWLOON.

The Kowloon Magistrate had before him this morning a Chinese who had been convicted on four occasions for returning from banishment and imprisoned several times for Jarceny.

The man was round guilty again on both charges, the theft in this instance being a jacket together with $15. Sentence of three months' hard labour was imposed on each charge, and defendant was ordered to receive in addition 18 strokes of the birch.

A Chinese had several of his ribs broken when he was knocked down by a motor lorry at Praya East yesterday morning. The driver of the vehicle alleged that the accident was due to the injured man's misfortune.

headline: GROWING GRAVITY.
text:
DISPUTE BETWEEN CHINA AND SOVIET.

HOSTILITIES NOT LIKELY.

The Diet re-opened this morning, after the New Year recess. Speeches were made by Viscount Kato, the Premier, and Baron Shidehara, K.E.E., the Foreign Minister.

Following their speeches this morning in the Upper House, Baron Sakatani grew attention to the growing gravity of the Sino-Russian situation and enquired about the "government's attitude." In reply, Baron Shideharstated that the matter was regarded purely as a Sino-Russian problem and unlikely to culminate in hostilities, though the Government was watching possible developments vigilantly test future action might be required.

Most of the morning papers offer no comment on the Sino-Russian friction, though the "Hochi" voices the opinion that the trouble is due to Chan Tsolin's desire to re-establish, his damaged prestige by stirring up Chinese national settlement in his favour.

The "Fleochii" forecasts in Chinese success, as the Soviet action is fettered by fear of damaging relation with Japan.

According to an “Asahi” despatch from Duiren, Chang Tso-lin ordered the arrest of M. Ivanov. President of the Chinese Eastern Railway, and the Mukden authorities to resume the railway service by force if necessary. A despatch to the “Asahi” from Harbin reports that the gravity is increasing and the Chinese troops are preparing to concentrate in Harbin in greater numbers.

According to Press reports, M. Kopp, the Soviet Ambassador to Japan, when interviewed, declared that "the Russian Government is prepared to back up its demands by force; if necessary meeting troops with troops."

In spite of all this, the vernacular papers generally indicate that the Japanese Government and people are maintaining a calm attitude.

headline: MILITARY ENCOURAGEMENT
text:
The outrages continue, the military leaders virtually encouraging them and evidently anxious to paralyse railway work in all sections. The lecture on February 1st at the Helena May Institute will be “The Story of Heligoland before and after the War”—not “Heavier-than-Air-Craft” as advertised. It is hoped that this lecture will be given at a later date.

headline: MEXICO'S LAWS.
text:
OWNERSHIP OF LANDS AND MINERALS.

Mexico City, Jan. 21. The new law regulating foreign ownership of lands, water, and minerals has been gazetted and comes into force today.

The latest development in the Mexican oil lands dispute is contained in an announcement by Mr. Guy Stevens, Director of the Association of Producers of Petroleum in Mexico, that the applications for injunctions recently filed by American oil companies against the new Petroleum Law have been refused by the First Supernumerary Court of Mexico.

Mexico City, Jan. 21. The British Minister, Mr. Esmond Ovey, visited the American Ambassador, Mr. Sheffield. It is believed that they discussed the respective British and American attitudes regarding the new Allen Land and Petroleum laws. It is understood that these attitudes are in perfect accord.

headline: RAILWAY WAGES
text:
DELEGATES: REJECT BOARD'S AWARD.

CRITICAL CONFERENCE

Trouble has again arisen in the railway world.

At to-day's conference of the branch delegates of the National Union of Railwaymen rejected the award of the National Wages Board which, after considering the Companies' claims for a reduction in wages and the men's counterclaims for increases, issued a report on December 9 practically maintaining the status quo. It is noteworthy that the men's leaders, Mr. J. H. Thomas (former

Though to-day's conference is generally regarded as the most critical since the last big strike, it is gathered that the decision merely reflects the movement for the re-opening of the negotiations, the delegates being not anxious to commit the Union to strike action.

The decision creates a delicate situation as the award is due to come into operation on February 1. The conference will again meet to-morrow to consider the next move.

Though it is believed that no decision for strike action will be taken until the Unions' Executive have met, the Companies have endeavoured to re-open the negotiations or secure a postponement of the application of the award.

headline: China / RUSH FOR PIGS.
text:
COLLISION WITH B. & S. STEAMEN

REPORTED CASUALTIES.

One or two men are said to have been drowned on Sunday night, following a collision in the harbour, but the Chinese reports of fatalities are contradicted by the official statement of the (China Navigation (E. & S.) s.s "Chinhua."

Local "Lans" (wholesale depots) commission stevedores to take delivery of live pigs, consigned to them, on the arrival of incoming steamers. Those who bring in the first lot from a ship get an extra thirty events per pig, as the loss landed earlier command the best sale.

As the "Chinhua" was entering hairboard about 10 p.m. on Sunday two sampans, both showing flares, tried to make fast while she was, under way, near "Green Island." Words passed in Chinese. It is believed that those in the sampans learned that the ship (coming from Bangkok, via Hoihow) had no pigs on board.

One of the sampans got in the way. There was a collision, sternly to stern end on. The sampam became a total wreck. A boat was put off in very quick time from the "Chinaia" in charge of a European officer but according to the statement of those on the other sampam the occupants of the damaged boat had been picked up. After it had been ascertained that there was nobody else in the water, the steamer proceeded. In this morning's vernacular papers it is stated that one of the stavedores has not been accounted for.

headline: CRISIS OVER?
text:
RAILWAY DELEGATES VOTE FOR AWARD.

A NARROW MAJORITY

...Rugby, Jan: 25.

At the meeting between representatives of the railway companies and of the National Union of Railwaymen, which was held this morning, there was a full discussion of the objections raised by the men to the award of the National Wages Board. As explained in previous messages the men object to the finding of the National Wages Board that men hereafter joining the railway service and not promoted shall receive only the basic wage of those grades to which they are appointed without cost of living bonus, and they ask for an assurance that the railway companies will accept the basic rates as an irreducible minimum. The exact tenor of the railway companies' reply has not been announced.

At a conference of railway-men's delegates this afternoon two resolutions were moved. One resolution was for refusing to accept the award and declaring a strike next Friday. The other was for acceptance of the award. By a very narrow majority the resolution accepting the award was adopted. It would appear therefore that the railway crisis is over.

headline: THE CRITICAL STAGE
text: London, Jan. 25. Critical negotiations between representatives of the railway companies and the N.U.R. were opened at Euston this morning in regard to the Union's demands. Several Branches of the Union have already adopted a resolution in favour of a national strike if the Union's demands are refused. At the conclusion of the negotiations the companies submitted a memorandum which the delegates' conference of railwaymen will consider.

headline: COMPANIES FIRM
text: At to-day's negotiations the railway companies declined to concede the points raised by the Railwaymen's Union. They pointed out that they accepted the findings of the Wages Board, which the Union repudiated a second time after the Union's representatives had signed the report. The companies intimated that if the Union persisted in this attitude they would be out-aged seriously to consider their attitude toward the Wages Board machinery which was being rendered "futile and farcical."

text:
Passionate speeches were delivered on both sides at the railwaymen's conference in debating the motion for a definite strike on Friday, which was ultimately rejected by 41 votes to 36. The outcome is regarded as a triumph for Mr. J. H. Thomas, who throughout strove to unhold the prestige of the Wages Board.
